title: Moving Forward in the Midst of Survival Mode
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Written after a month in which his wife's illness upended his schedule, this retrospective asks how a teacher keeps making professional progress without betraying life priorities. Stuart first argues that educators should not sacrifice their families on the altar of career success, because teaching is a calling but not one that outranks marriage and parenting, and because burnt-out teachers serve students worse. He then audits honestly what he dropped and what he finished in January, framing many omissions as deliberate triage rather than failure. The core of the post is seven survival tactics: accept help, clear two-minute tasks, delay projects without firm deadlines, ship work that must be done even if imperfect, take the smallest next step, keep doing hard things, and protect sleep. The move is to turn a personal hard season into a practical, permission-giving framework for the profession's workload problem.
points: Professional priorities should never outrank family commitments, and overwork does not make a teacher better at the job.
Treat a crisis as a triage exercise: separate the deadlines that cannot move from the good ideas that can safely wait.
Defeat perfectionism by drafting early, then sending a finished rather than flawless product.
Sleep belongs in a teacher's professional development plan, since chronic late-night grading signals a sustainability problem rather than a grit deficit.
Stuart notes that the expectation of grit placed only on students is a hollow one when teachers do not also do hard things themselves.
quotes: First and most pragmatically, it is simply not necessary to sacrifice one’s personal life in order to promote the long-term flourishing of our students. Putting all our time into this job does not inherently mean doing it better.

On a deeper level, though, we simply owe our families more than we owe our students. When I married Crystal, I made a vow to her to love her unconditionally, daily, and with multitudinous acts of love. I’ve made no like vows to my students.
Here’s the takeaway: be open to the help of others. I’ve had to grow into a man who can say, “Yes, thank you,” when someone offers help. Teachers too often are fiercely independent.
When things go wrong and your working hours take a huge hit, it’s time to triage. What must get done by a certain deadline and can’t be moved?
Here’s the takeaway: Defy perfectionism — it seeks to enslave you. Get your work done and get it in front of the eyes that need to see it.

Nothing is more painfully ironic to me than schools where the word “grit” is thrown at kids because it’s an easy way of placing all the responsibility on them. When grit is something we expect only from our students, it’s going to fail.
Some of you tell me things like, “I’m up until midnight grading every night.” That is not sustainable. That is not a situation in which you need more grit; it’s one in which you need more sleep.
